## What a brown dwarf is
A brown dwarf is an object between the giant planets and the smallest stars. Brown dwarfs form like stars, from a collapsing cloud of gas, but never become massive enough to sustain the fusion of hydrogen in their cores. They shine through gravitational contraction, as gas giant planets do. Brown dwarfs of sufficient mass fuse deuterium (heavy hydrogen) for a time, but this stops after a few million years. Because they are cool, they emit most of their light in the infrared.
Sources: nasa-gl229b, nasa-webb-brown-dwarf, jpl-identity-crisis, nasa-webb-young-bd

## Mass range: the sources do not agree
The upper limit is the mass needed to sustain hydrogen fusion, about 8 percent of the Sun's mass or roughly 75 to 80 Jupiter masses. The lower limit is stated differently by different sources: 15 to 75 Jupiter masses (NASA StarChild), 10 to 70 Jupiter masses (JPL), 1 to 8 percent of the Sun's mass (NASA Webb article), and 13.6 to 80 Jupiter masses with the deuterium-burning limit near 13 Jupiter masses as the lower bound (Gan et al. 2025). Webb observations suggest that objects formed like stars may exist down to 2-3 Jupiter masses. The disagreement reflects two definitions, one by deuterium fusion and one by how the object formed. Q-FIT reports the range together with the source it comes from.
Sources: nasa-starchild-bd, jpl-identity-crisis, nasa-webb-young-bd, gan-2025-apjl, nasa-webb-brown-dwarf

## Spectral types L, T and Y
Brown dwarfs are grouped by temperature into spectral types: L dwarfs are the warmest group, T dwarfs are cooler, and Y dwarfs are the coolest, with surface temperatures of about 200 to 500 kelvin. The Y class was discovered in 2011 with NASA's Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE).
Sources: cfa-y-dwarfs

## First detection
The first unambiguous brown dwarf, Gliese 229B, was found in October 1994 as a companion of the red dwarf Gliese 229 and confirmed a year later. Its mass was estimated at 20 to 50 Jupiter masses, and its atmosphere resembles Jupiter's in composition.
Sources: nasa-gl229b

## SPHEREx and brown dwarfs
A study published in The Astrophysical Journal and reported by NASA on 8 October 2026 used SPHEREx to study 37 nearby brown dwarfs, measuring the brightness of each in 102 colors to build a spectrum. The spectra show water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane, and the sample spans temperatures from roughly 2,200 degrees Celsius down to about -20 degrees Celsius. The team reports that thousands more brown dwarfs are being analysed and that models have difficulty matching the data where clouds change. Observing from space avoids the wavelengths absorbed by water vapour in Earth's atmosphere. This is a published result of the SPHEREx team, not something Q-FIT measured.
Sources: nasa-spherex-brown-dwarfs
